title: The whole in a grain
hookLine: a world in a grain of dust, all time in a moment

lines: WORLDS IN A SPECK OF DUST.
cards: One grain of rice is left on the table after dinner. A thumb is already on its way to brush it off. The Flower Garland Sutra would like that thumb to pause.

It says something that sounds impossible: inside a single speck of dust there are whole worlds, with Buddhas teaching in them, and inside one moment there are ages upon ages of time. Yesterday a tower held towers.
Today it gets smaller, and stranger.

teach.h: WORLDS INSIDE A SPECK OF DUST.
teach.b: Start with space. The sutra pictures a speck of dust, almost too small to see, and inside it, worlds beyond counting, each with its lands and its beings and a Buddha teaching there. Here's the careful part.
The speck doesn't swell up to make room, and the worlds don't shrink down to fit. Each stays exactly its own size, and still the one holds the many.

Huayan teachers in China had a phrase for this: big and small don't obstruct each other. Then time. One instant of thought holds vast ages, and vast ages fit inside one instant, and neither is squeezed.
Past, present and future can be found in a single moment, the way the whole net is found in a single jewel. Why would anyone say this?
Because in this way of seeing, nothing has a fixed size or a fixed edge of its own.

A grain of rice isn't a little sealed box. It's made of a field, of rain and sun and soil, of hands that planted and hands that harvested, of the trucks and the store and the pot. That's the gentle version.
The sutra goes further: the grain isn't only linked to everything; the whole is present in it. So the small thing on the table, about to be brushed away, isn't small in the way it looks.
That can change how a crumb gets swept, or how one ordinary minute gets spent.

how: Huayan teachers in China drew on these passages of the Flower Garland Sutra to describe a world in which the small and the large, and a moment and an age, contain each other without obstruction.

games.q: what does “the whole in a grain” mean?
o: worlds inside a speck of dust, and ages in a moment
a monk's vow never to waste a single grain of food
a tiny seed that grows into a great tree in time

games.q: the whole in a grain: tap the pairs.

nothing changes size. the speck stays a speck, and still holds them.
the sutra says the same about time

games.q: you're reading the Flower Garland, and worlds are said to fit inside a speck of dust. how does the sutra make room?
games.why: neither changes. the speck stays a speck, the worlds stay worlds. Huayan teachers said big and small don't obstruct each other.

practice: Put something tiny where you can see it: a grain of rice or salt, a crumb, a speck of dust. Look at it longer than feels normal, its color and its edges.
Then let it open: where did it come from, who touched it on the way, what weather made it? Let this one grain be enough.

wordCard.voice: The whole in a grain. The Flower Garland's teaching that a speck of dust holds worlds, and one moment holds ages, without either changing size. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the smallest particle, a speck finer than dust.

carryVoice: Your line: a world in a grain. One ordinary minute can hold more than it seems. Go gently.
